video_title: The ‘Everywhere All At Once’ Cybersecurity Crisis | The Ezra Klein Show
gist: Former NYT cyber reporter turned VC Nicole Perlroth tells Ezra Klein that AI (catalyzed by Anthropic's Mythos and open-source attack frameworks) has flipped cyber economics toward attackers at machine speed, so the 'digital deficit' of decades of insecure software is coming due — producing self-inflicted outages from rushed patching (FAA, Microsoft, Apple, Chase), overwhelmed incident responders, and deepfake social engineering. She expects a painful, longer-than-18-month transition where AI eventually aids defense, with the have-nots (critical infrastructure, mid-market firms) most exposed.

themes.theme: AI-driven offense: machine-speed hacking and the 'digital deficit'

insights.claim: AI has collapsed the time and skill needed to find and exploit vulnerabilities, putting defenders on 'the attacker's clock' and forcing software makers and enterprises to patch faster than ever.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Demand for vulnerability management, patch automation and security tooling should structurally rise as patch cadence accelerates.
insights.quote: We're all suddenly living on the attackers's clock.

insights.claim: Decades of 'move fast and break things' and 'software eats the world' embedded flawed, vulnerable software everywhere; with AI able to exploit it at machine speed, this 'digital deficit' is now coming due, unlike the fiscal deficit which remains deferred.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Frame cyber spend as servicing accumulated technical debt — a multi-year, non-discretionary budget line rather than a cyclical one.
insights.quote: The digital deficit is coming due right now because we have this perfect storm and collision with AI capabilities.

insights.claim: Anthropic's Mythos model, released in April only to a limited set of businesses and institutions because it was so capable at hacking, marked a phase shift; AI subsequently helped find a vulnerability in PHP (supporting roughly 70% of websites) and new vulnerabilities are being reported in Java.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Foundational software layers (PHP, Java, Linux) are now in scope for AI-discovered bugs — expect waves of critical CVEs and emergency patch cycles across enterprises.

insights.claim: The binding constraint on hacking used to be the small number of highly skilled humans; frontier-model capabilities migrating into unguarded open-source models effectively create a limitless supply of skilled hackers, so the cost of a very good attack has plummeted while defense costs have not.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Offense/defense economics have shifted structurally toward attackers; insurers, incident responders and security vendors face rising loss frequency and demand.
insights.quote: there's almost no limit on how many hackers there are

insights.claim: An open-source multi-agent penetration-testing framework (transcribed as 'Rex'/'RTX'), built ostensibly for enterprise self-testing across commercial and open-source models, has been adopted by attackers to automate the kill chain from discovery through privilege escalation to exfiltration; the FBI issued a flash advisory that groups including Chinese actors are using it against finance, healthcare, manufacturing and telecom.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Dual-use open-source offensive tooling means sector-wide, automated targeting — watch FBI/CISA advisories as leading indicators of breach waves in specific sectors.

insights.claim: Ransomware over the past two years moved from manual workflows (buying access, screening victims for cyber insurance, negotiating payment) to ad hoc automation; this month it shifted to 'push the attack button' agentic operations covering most of the kill chain.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Cyber insurers face rising frequency and correlated risk; insured firms are explicitly preferred targets.
insights.quote: It is very much entering a new age of push the attack button and come back with everything

insights.claim: The old security doctrine of 'don't be the slowest gazelle' no longer works because AI agents can scan and attack everyone at once, so being merely more secure than peers no longer deters attackers.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Mid-tier security posture is no longer a defensible strategy; baseline security spend must rise across the long tail of firms.
insights.quote: don't be the slowest gazelle in the savannah

insights.claim: The capabilities gap between US intelligence (e.g., Stuxnet-level operations) and other actors like Iran, North Korea and cybercriminals has closed; China pivoted from IP theft to pre-positioning in US critical infrastructure, and now the 'everything everywhere all at once' scenario applies to any actor, not just China.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Geopolitical tail risk (e.g., Taiwan) now carries a critical-infrastructure disruption component; national-security cyber budgets should rise.

insights.claim: AI-enabled attacks run without human fatigue, across time zones and without regard to patching schedules, so organizations should expect continuous automated scanning of every exposed system.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Favor always-on, automated defense (exposure management, continuous monitoring) over periodic assessment models.

themes.theme: Outage wave: patching risk and fragile legacy infrastructure

insights.claim: The near-simultaneous outages at the FAA (nationwide ground stop), Microsoft Outlook, Apple iCloud and Chase appear to be self-inflicted — caused by rushed upgrades and patches to harden systems against AI attacks — rather than malicious attacks, though full postmortems are pending.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Expect more operational outages from accelerated patching; this is a new operational-risk category for large tech and financial firms.
insights.quote: These were sort of selfowned, right?

insights.claim: Finding and exploiting a vulnerability is now easy with AI, but fixing it remains hard because patches must be tested to avoid breaking complex systems — this asymmetry guarantees more breakage as patch speed rises.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Software testing, change management, and resilience/rollback tooling become higher-value as patch velocity increases.
insights.quote: There's no easy button for patching.

insights.claim: The coming period will be a 'software Beirut' in which systems people rely on daily flicker on and off, with outages and attacks becoming the new normal.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Price in higher frequency of service disruptions; resilience, backup, and redundancy vendors benefit.
insights.quote: things that we were just accustomed to working day in and day out will start flickering on and off

insights.claim: Much critical infrastructure runs unsupported software that cannot receive patches at all, and patching it requires planned outages that may happen only once a year or less, making a patch as disruptive as an attack.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Legacy modernization and rip-and-replace programs in utilities and government are underfunded but increasingly urgent.
insights.quote: sometimes once a year is optimistic

insights.claim: Water treatment facilities rarely have in-house IT, rely on remote access by outside contractors to monitor chemical levels, and this remote access creates openings that Iranian hackers have probed.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Water/utility OT security is a specific under-protected niche; watch for regulation and funding mandates.

insights.claim: Government procurement is so slow that by the time agencies acquire technology they wanted two years earlier, it is already outdated; the FAA's old routers and software and the IRS master file running on archaic languages illustrate the problem.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Government IT modernization is a large but slow addressable market; vendors with procurement expertise hold an edge.

insights.claim: Bureaucratic incentives make it worse to be the person who broke a system by updating it than to be the one who failed to secure it against a foreign hacking force, so the needed self-disruption (simulating attacks on ourselves) is systematically avoided.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Expect public-sector hardening to lag private sector; critical-infrastructure risk remains elevated longer than headlines suggest.
insights.quote: in a bureaucratic logic way it is worse to be the one who broke it

insights.claim: A McKinsey report frames the core enterprise cyber problem as 'organizational latency': CEOs and security leaders say cultures, systems, vendors and laws are not designed to operate at AI speed or take the risks updates require.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Services and automation that reduce organizational latency (not just new technical controls) address the real bottleneck.
insights.quote: what they call organizational latency

insights.claim: Much infrastructure is 'vendor over vendor over vendor' stitched together (e.g., blame for the FAA outage pointing to L3Harris), and large enterprises are not using purchasing power to force vendors to test software for flaws before release — something expected to change.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Vendor-security attestation and software supply-chain assurance requirements are likely to tighten; a potential liability risk for infrastructure vendors.
insights.quote: vendor over vendor over vendor stitched together

themes.theme: Defender capacity crunch and cyber haves vs. have-nots

insights.claim: Incident response firms are out of capacity and turning away breach victims — even nation-state-level emergencies — and incidents are reportedly up 50% from the busiest month ever recorded.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Strong demand and pricing power for incident response services; capacity constraints imply growth limited by talent.
insights.quote: By some accounts, they're up 50% right now from the busiest month we've ever seen.

insights.claim: At CrowdStrike, executives such as the president, who have not worked an incident in years, are being pulled into triaging security incidents because of demand.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Signal of surging services demand at a listed security leader (CRWD); watch services revenue and commentary for confirmation.

insights.claim: CISOs at Fortune 100 companies report facing autonomous attacks all day, every day, some considering retirement, and a major supply-chain company reported being extorted for the third time in one week.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Attack volume is far larger than what reaches the news; expect breach disclosures and cyber-related earnings hits to rise.
insights.quote: We are up against autonomous attacks all day, every day

insights.claim: Banks and financial services treat cyber as existential (e.g., JPMorgan would lose customers if accounts were wiped) and have effectively a blank check, while firms just below the Fortune 500 lack resources and see no ROI on security, preferring to spend on AI rollouts or new products.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Risk concentrates in the mid-market and smaller firms; large banks are relatively hardened while the long tail is exposed.
insights.quote: there is no ROI on cyber security

insights.claim: Anthropic's Project Glass Wing gave roughly 40 of the most important internet firms early access to Mythos to harden defenses, raising the question of whether customers of smaller email providers or banks (vs. Microsoft, Google, Wells Fargo, Bank of America) take on more risk.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Early access to frontier defensive AI may widen the security moat of the largest platforms and banks, favoring scale incumbents.

insights.claim: Under the Trump administration, DOGE cuts hit CISA, which led critical-infrastructure resilience efforts prioritized under Biden; CISA still lacks a Senate-confirmed leader and staff brought in to advance those efforts were reportedly fired.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Reduced federal coordination raises critical-infrastructure tail risk and may shift burden (and spend) to private operators and states.

themes.theme: AI on defense and investable security solutions

insights.claim: AI is a source of hope on defense: new tools let small and medium enterprises map their whole environment for gaps (e.g., CrowdStrike not installed on every endpoint, missing MFA on an internet-exposed server) and let large enterprises match their security stack against live threat intelligence to prioritize and automate fixes.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: AI-native exposure management and automated remediation for SMBs and enterprises is an attractive investment category.

insights.claim: Colonial Pipeline was compromised because a former employee was never deprovisioned and MFA was not properly installed — exactly the hygiene gaps AI is good at detecting — but for now AI finds and exploits vulnerabilities faster than defenders can patch.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Identity hygiene (deprovisioning, MFA coverage) tooling has clear, demonstrable value; the near-term window still favors attackers.
insights.quote: we're in this window where it's able to find vulnerabilities and exploit them much much quicker than we can patch

insights.claim: Perlroth, who left journalism in 2022 to start a cyber mission fund (Silver Buckshot Ventures), made her first investment in a deepfake detection company because deepfakes and disinformation are her top worry.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Deepfake detection and authenticity verification are a VC-backed thesis from a cyber-specialist investor.
insights.quote: my first investment was in a deep fake detection company

insights.claim: Truth and human authenticity will become the most valuable commodity in the future.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Provenance, identity verification and authenticity infrastructure could command premium value.
insights.quote: truth, human authenticity is going to be the most valuable commodity in the future

themes.theme: Social engineering, deepfakes and the low-trust internet

insights.claim: AI is making phishing and social engineering dramatically more convincing, including voice-cloned fake-kidnapping calls that have led people to wire money; credential compromise via people can bypass even well-locked-down software.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Human-layer security (verification protocols, anti-fraud, training) becomes a bigger share of cyber risk and spend.

insights.claim: In one week there were three cases at major Fortune 500 companies where a deepfaked executive, usually the CFO, authorized fraudulent wire payments or obtained credentials via a fake IT department, leading to breaches.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Payment-authorization fraud via audio deepfakes is a live corporate loss vector; favors out-of-band verification and fraud-detection vendors.

insights.claim: Organizations and families should adopt code words to verify identity on calls; social engineering is 'the hardest problem of all' and will get harder with deepfakes.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Cheap procedural controls matter; expect enterprise adoption of verification protocols and related products.
insights.quote: this is the hardest problem of all

insights.claim: The internet is shifting from a high-trust back to a low-trust environment within the next 12–24 months, where emails, audio and video can no longer be assumed authentic unless from a party one has strong reason to trust.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Trusted brands and verification layers gain value; anonymous/long-tail commerce may face friction.

insights.claim: People are simultaneously extremely skeptical and extremely trusting: they say they distrust institutions but act credulously because operating without trust is too costly in time and attention — while increasingly outsourcing their lives to AI agents (e.g., Muse for working mothers).
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Adoption of AI agents is unlikely to be slowed by security fears; trust tends to accrue to large incumbents like Amazon, Google and Facebook over small firms.
insights.quote: they don't believe anybody, but in a weird way, they also believe everybody

insights.claim: Google Threat Intelligence Group warned that the era of autonomous cyber attacks is here and seen in the wild, and that AI is being used to stand up hundreds of legitimate-looking social media personas to spread disinformation.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Platform integrity and bot-detection are rising risks/costs for social media companies.

insights.claim: Individual protection checklist: keep printed bank statements and copies of critical documents, use unique passwords (password managers for most accounts, though Perlroth avoids them for email, brokerage and bank), prefer passkeys or authenticator apps over SMS MFA which is repeatedly compromised, avoid links from strangers, and identify and harden or take offline what is most precious.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Passkey/authenticator adoption and backup solutions are secular beneficiaries of rising consumer threat awareness.
insights.quote: SMS, MFA has been compromised over and over again.

insights.claim: Anthropic deputy CISO Jason Clinton argues the world faces an ~18-month window of pain after which systems will be more secure and reliable; Perlroth considers this 'incredibly optimistic' because it assumes rip-and-replace of archaic systems without cascading supply-chain failures while under constant AI attack.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Don't assume the disruption window is short; position for a multi-year elevated cyber-spend and outage-risk regime.
insights.quote: I think that is incredibly optimistic.

insights.claim: The 'soft' challenges — political will, budgets, leadership, resource allocation and finding people who understand legacy systems — are consistently underestimated and are the real bottleneck, since technical controls alone would have solved cybersecurity two decades ago.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Cyber talent scarcity and services capacity are key constraints; labor-saving security automation has strong demand.

insights.claim: Eventually AI will be used to write more secure code (e.g., eliminating buffer overflows), leading to a better place after a painful transition.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Long-term, secure-by-design AI code generation could reduce vulnerability supply — a tailwind for AI coding tools with security features.

insights.claim: Policy proposals: regulation requiring software testing before release (especially for critical infrastructure), and a cyber 'tour of duty' where companies lend top security staff to have-nots like water treatment facilities in exchange for tax credits, bonuses or student debt relief.
insights.speaker: Nicole Perlroth
insights.so_what: Watch for secure-by-design regulation and tax-incentive programs that could shift liability onto software vendors.
insights.quote: ultimately it just comes down to incentives
